params.question: Which of the following best explains why an ABO-incompatible transfusion can cause intravascular haemolysis even on the very first exposure?

answers.text: Anti-A and anti-B are IgG antibodies transferred passively from the mother during fetal life

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ABO antibodies are IgM, not IgG. Unlike anti-D in the Rh system, they do not require prior sensitisation and are not maternally derived — they are natural isoagglutinins present from infancy.

answers.text: Pre-existing IgM isoagglutinins in the recipient's plasma activate complement immediately upon encountering incompatible donor red cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. By Landsteiner's Law, plasma contains antibodies against whichever ABO antigens are absent from one's own red cells. These natural IgM antibodies, driven by cross-reactive environmental antigens from gut bacteria and food, activate the classical complement pathway on first contact — no prior exposure to foreign blood is needed.

answers.text: The recipient's T lymphocytes mount a direct cytotoxic attack on the mismatched donor cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ABO-incompatible haemolysis is antibody- and complement-mediated (humoral immunity), not T-cell–mediated. Cell-mediated immunity plays no significant role in acute ABO transfusion reactions.

answers.text: Donor plasma antibodies destroy the recipient's own red blood cells through an autoimmune mechanism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In an ABO-incompatible transfusion, it is the recipient's pre-existing antibodies that destroy the donor's red cells, not the reverse. The small volume of donor plasma is diluted and rarely causes significant haemolysis of recipient cells.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key is Landsteiner's Law: your plasma already contains IgM antibodies against whichever ABO antigens your own cells lack. These IgM antibodies activate complement immediately on contact with incompatible red cells, causing intravascular haemolysis on first exposure.
Well done. Natural IgM isoagglutinins and complement activation are the basis of immediate ABO-incompatible intravascular haemolysis — no prior sensitisation is needed.

params.question: One 450 mL whole-blood donation is separated into four components. Which combination correctly pairs a blood component with its storage requirements?

answers.text: Packed red blood cells at 20–24 °C for 42 days

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Packed red blood cells must be stored at 2–6 °C, not at room temperature. Room temperature (20–24 °C) is the correct storage condition for platelet concentrates, which last only 5 days.

answers.text: Platelet concentrates at 2–6 °C with continuous agitation for 5 days

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Platelets require room temperature (20–24 °C), not refrigeration. The continuous agitation and 5-day shelf life are correct, but the temperature is wrong. Remember: Platelets room-5.

answers.text: Packed red blood cells at 2–6 °C for 42 days with SAGM additive

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. SAGM (saline, adenine, glucose, mannitol) additive solution extends packed RBC shelf life to 42 days at 2–6 °C. The mnemonic is Red: 2-6-42.
Fresh frozen plasma must be stored at minus 18 °C or colder, not at refrigerator temperature. At minus 18 °C it lasts 12 months — the mnemonic is Plasma: freeze-12.

overallFeedback.feedback: Each blood component has specific storage requirements. Packed RBCs: 2–6 °C for 42 days (SAGM additive). Platelets: 20–24 °C with continuous agitation for 5 days. FFP: minus 18 °C for 12 months.
Excellent. Remember the storage mnemonic: Red 2-6-42, Platelets room-5, Plasma freeze-12.

interactions.label: The most common infectious cause of transfusion-related death is bacterial conta

params.question: The most common infectious cause of transfusion-related death is bacterial contamination of platelet concentrates, not viral infection.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. While most students assume viral infections like HIV or hepatitis are the leading infectious cause, room-temperature platelet storage allows bacterial proliferation from skin flora at the needle site, making bacterial contamination the most common infectious cause of transfusion-related death.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Room-temperature storage of platelets allows skin flora from the phlebotomy site to multiply to dangerous levels. Despite rigorous viral screening with five mandatory tests, bacterial contamination remains the leading infectious cause of transfusion-related death.

interactions.label: A 70-year-old patient develops acute dyspnoea and bilateral pulmonary infiltrate

params.question: A 70-year-old patient develops acute dyspnoea and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-ray during a red cell transfusion. Which single clinical finding best distinguishes transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) from transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO)?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fever can occur in both TRALI and febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reactions. It is not a reliable feature for distinguishing TRALI from TACO; jugular venous pressure and BNP are more discriminating.
Both TRALI and TACO may show partial improvement with oxygen. The response to oxygen does not reliably differentiate the two conditions at the bedside.

answers.text: Jugular venous pressure — normal in TRALI, raised in TACO

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. TRALI is non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema caused by donor antibodies activating recipient pulmonary neutrophils — JVP remains normal. TACO is volume overload with a raised JVP. This single bedside sign is the most reliable discriminator.

answers.text: Onset within the first 5 minutes of transfusion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: TRALI typically develops within 6 hours of transfusion, not necessarily in the first few minutes. Very rapid onset within minutes is more characteristic of acute haemolytic or anaphylactic reactions, not TRALI specifically.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key distinction is jugular venous pressure. TRALI is immune-mediated non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (normal JVP), while TACO is simple volume overload (raised JVP). Both cause bilateral infiltrates and dyspnoea, but JVP tells them apart at the bedside.
Well done. TRALI (immune-mediated, normal JVP) versus TACO (volume overload, raised JVP) — this bedside distinction is a high-yield exam question and a critical clinical decision point.

interactions.label: A multiply alloimmunised patient with a rare blood group is scheduled for electi

params.question: A multiply alloimmunised patient with a rare blood group is scheduled for elective surgery. Which is the primary advantage of using autologous transfusion in this scenario?

answers.text: Autologous blood has a longer shelf life than allogeneic donor units

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Autologous pre-donated units follow the same storage rules and shelf-life limits as allogeneic blood. The advantage lies in immunological safety, not storage duration.

answers.text: It completely eliminates the risk of transfusion-transmitted infection and alloimmunisation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Since the patient receives their own blood, there is zero risk of acquiring a new transfusion-transmitted infection or forming new alloantibodies — especially valuable in patients who are already multiply alloimmunised or have rare blood groups.

answers.text: It avoids the need for any pre-operative planning or blood collection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: On the contrary, autologous transfusion requires careful planning. Preoperative autologous donation needs weeks of advance collection, and cell salvage or haemodilution requires specialised equipment at the time of surgery.

answers.text: It provides a greater haemoglobin increment per unit than allogeneic blood

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The haemoglobin increment per unit is similar for autologous and allogeneic packed red cells. The advantage is not in efficacy per unit but in eliminating immunological and infectious risks.

overallFeedback.feedback: The primary advantage of autologous transfusion — whether preoperative donation, acute normovolaemic haemodilution, or intraoperative cell salvage — is the complete elimination of transfusion-transmitted infection and alloimmunisation risk, since the patient receives only their own blood.

Correct. Autologous transfusion eliminates transfusion-transmitted infection and alloimmunisation risk entirely — ideal for patients with rare blood groups, multiple alloantibodies, or religious objections to donor blood.
